mcqs.question: What specifically separates a "refactor" from a "rewrite"?
options: A refactor is done by a junior engineer, a rewrite by a senior one
A refactor must preserve observable behavior — same inputs, same outputs — while a rewrite is free to change it
A refactor can only be applied to methods shorter than 20 lines
A refactor never touches more than one file, while a rewrite always does
mcqs.explanation: The defining property of refactoring is behavior preservation, verified by tests — that's what makes it safe to do incrementally. Seniority, method length, and file count aren't part of the definition; a refactor can span many files as long as behavior stays identical.

mcqs.question: Why are Extract Method and Extract Class considered low-risk refactors?
options: They are always performed automatically by the IDE with no human review needed
They only apply to code that already has 100% test coverage
They require deleting the original code entirely before writing the replacement
They change where logic lives and what it's called, without changing the logic itself
mcqs.explanation: Both refactors relocate and rename code without altering its actual logic, which is exactly why they carry low risk of behavior change. They don't require full coverage beforehand (though tests make verification easier), IDEs can assist but human review still matters, and neither refactor is about deleting code outright before replacing it.

mcqs.question: What's the concrete benefit of Replace Conditional with Polymorphism when a new type is added later?
options: Adding the new type requires no code changes anywhere in the system
It eliminates the need for any interface or shared contract between types
Adding a new subclass with its own method is enough — no existing switch statement needs to be found and edited
It makes the codebase run faster than a switch statement would
mcqs.explanation: The real payoff is that new behavior extends the system via a new subclass instead of requiring edits to existing conditional logic scattered across methods — this is the open/closed principle in action. It still requires writing the new subclass (not zero changes), it relies on a shared interface rather than eliminating one, and there's no inherent runtime speed claim here.

mcqs.question: In the step-by-step `processOrder` refactor, what does extracting `validate` and `calculateTotal` into their own methods make possible that the original 12-line method didn't?
options: The application starts up faster because fewer methods are compiled together
Each piece — validation, total calculation, persistence — can be read and tested independently instead of requiring the whole method traced at once
The database calls become unnecessary
It guarantees the discount logic can never contain a bug
mcqs.explanation: The value is readability and independent testability — you can verify `calculateTotal` without also exercising validation or persistence. There's no startup-speed effect from this kind of extraction, the database save is still needed, and no refactor can guarantee bug-free logic — it only makes bugs easier to find and isolate.

mcqs.question: You're about to refactor a smelly, untested method that you believe you understand well from reading it. What's the risk in skipping a characterization test?
options: There is no real risk — reading the code carefully is equivalent to testing it
The refactor will fail to compile without a test present
Edge cases the method handles in production but that aren't obvious from a read-through can silently change behavior without anyone noticing
Characterization tests are only needed for methods longer than 500 lines
mcqs.explanation: Reading is not verification — production edge cases (an empty list, a null field, a boundary date) are exactly what a careful read can miss, and a characterization test catches a behavior change immediately instead of letting it ship silently. Compilation is unaffected by the absence of a test, and there's no length threshold that makes characterization tests unnecessary for shorter methods.
